title: Short Stuff: Killing a Dead Body
summary: Short Stuff episode on whether a person can be legally murdered after already being dead, and how courts handle it. Josh and Chuck open with banter about Magnolia and a fictional Magnolia vignette (Sidney Barringer, a suicide attempt ruled a murder-related case) that they note is based on a story by Don Harper Mills. They then cover the legal concept of "legal impossibility" versus intent, using the 1986 French case of Chirou and Pédéros (Pederot) who attacked Wilkins after he was already unconscious, the 1975 New York case of Melvin Dlugash (Delugash), a Toronto police shooting case, and a 2014 Melbourne mercy-killing case involving Daniel Darrington and Matt Scassie. The consistent conclusion is that murder of a corpse is impossible, but attempted murder can be charged based on intent.

segments.title: Opening banter and Magnolia vignette
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about being alive, then discuss Magnolia and Ricky Jay's narration of a vignette about a man who jumps from a window and is killed by a shotgun blast from his mother. Chuck notes the story is not true and comes from Don Harper Mills's 1987 banquet story.

segments.title: Vignette as illustration of coroner rulings
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how new evidence can change a medical examiner's ruling on cause of death, and frame the episode question of whether one can murder someone already dead.

segments.summary: Brief teaser before the ad break, promising talk of Boogie Nights and Heart Eight.

segments.title: French Chirou and Pédéros case
segments.summary: Chirou beat and strangled Wilkins with an iron bar, then the next day Pédéros beat and strangled the apparently still-living Wilkins with a glass bottle. The medical examiner found Chirou had killed him, raising the question of Pédéros's liability for acting on a corpse.

segments.title: Legal impossibility versus intent
segments.summary: The defense argued legal impossibility barred guilt, while others argued intent governs. The French court looked for precedent, and the hosts note the New York case as relevant.

segments.title: Delugash New York 1975 case
segments.summary: In a 1975 New York City apartment, Joe Bush shot Michael Geller three times, then Melvin Dlugash fired five more shots into Geller's head. Dlugash was initially convicted of murder but the conviction was overturned because the prosecution could not prove Geller was alive when shot. The court said intent, not actual possibility, is what matters.

segments.title: Toronto police shooting case
segments.summary: A Toronto police officer shot a knife-wielding man three times, then shot him more after he fell. The jury would not convict of murder because the shots were in the line of duty, but the later shots could support attempted murder.

segments.title: Melbourne 2014 mercy killing case
segments.summary: In Melbourne in 2014, Daniel Darrington shot Matt Scassie after a struggle over a gun, then shot him again as a mercy. The jury acquitted him of murder but convicted him of attempted murder because he believed Scassie was alive.

segments.title: Takeaways and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts conclude that if someone might be alive, call an ambulance, and joke about how movies depict finishing off people. The episode closes with the iHeartRadio production credit.
